samples.unmet_requirement: A predominantly horizontal single-touch swipe starting on an interactive control must leave the step index unchanged; the touch-event path instead advances the step.

samples.rationale: The source corroborates the reported touch swipe changing step index 4 to 5. Window-level touch handlers record every starting target and execute swipe navigation without excluding interactive controls. The interactive-target guard applies only to keyboard events. The mode toggle is a button whose activation changes only mode, so the step-control exception does not apply. Failure on the touch path alone violates the requirement.
samples.unmet_requirement: A predominantly horizontal single-touch swipe starting on an interactive control at an interior step must leave the step index unchanged when delivered as touch events.

subcomponents.title: Verification tooling robustness

criteria.rationale: scripts/verify.mjs wraps preview start and browser launch in try/finally, and startPreview's stop() SIGTERMs the vite child directly (SIGKILL fallback) and awaits its exit. scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs does not do this. It calls startPreview and then chromium.launch() at lines 136-137, before the try block that starts at line 141. If the browser launch fails, preview.stop() never runs and the vite preview child is left running. The bootstrap template copies are byte-identical (enforced by the drift test), so they have the same defect.
evidence: inspect-presentation.mjs main(): `const preview = await startPreview(root)` and `const browser = await chromium.launch()` both precede `try {` and its `finally { await browser.close(); await preview.…
verify.mjs main(): `preview = await startPreview(root)` and `chromium.launch()` sit inside try, with `finally { await browser?.close(); await preview?.stop() }`
lib.mjs startPreview().stop() kills the spawned child itself, not an npm wrapper
judging basis: consensus-fail

criteria.rationale: startPreview polls the server with fetch against a 20s deadline, aborts if the child exits early, and stops the child on timeout. It never parses printed output, so the ANSI and chunk-splitting clause does not apply. Both scripts await runBuild before startPreview (verify always; inspect unless --skip-build is passed).
evidence: lib.mjs startPreview: `const deadline = Date.now() + timeoutMs` loop, `if (child.exitCode !== null) throw`, final `await stop(); throw new Error('did not become ready')`
verify.mjs main(): `await runBuild(root)` completes before `startPreview(root)`
inspect-presentation.mjs main(): the build is awaited before `startPreview` unless --skip-build is given
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The template verify.mjs does not take a slug. It renders every slug returned by readRegistrySlugs. The reference outline is optional: it is loaded only if scripts/reference-outline.json exists, and that file is not in the bootstrap. The template contains no sample titles, captions or routes. The template inspect script takes the slug as an argument and exits 2 with a clear message for an unregistered slug before building or previewing. The bootstrap integration test runs verify on a scaffolded project with smoke and quoted slugs.
evidence: bootstrap verify.mjs: `for (const slug of slugs) await renderPresentation(...)`, `reference?.slug === slug ? reference : null`
bootstrap inspect-presentation.mjs: `if (!readRegistrySlugs(root).includes(slug)) { console.error(... not registered ...); process.exit(2) }`
bootstrap.test.mjs INT-001 expects 'smoke: rendered 2 steps' and 'quoted: rendered 2 steps'
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: inspect-presentation.mjs reads `Number(getAttribute('data-step-count'))` and loops `for (i < count)` with no check for zero, NaN or missing. A NaN or 0 count captures nothing, writes a report, prints '0 screenshots written' and exits 0, so it can report success with zero captures. Before each capture it also never reads data-step-index to confirm it equals i. It only waits for the index after pressing ArrowRight.

The capture loop calls waitSettled and screenshot without comparing data-step-index to i
The end of main() prints the screenshot count and warnings and never fails when captures.length is 0
judging basis: consensus-fail

criteria.rationale: Titles, captions, order and step count are read from the rendered page via [data-presentation-step-title] and [data-presentation-step-caption]. But the registration check does not use the rendered page. `readRegistrySlugs` matches `/slug:\s*['"]([^'"]+)['"]/g` over the text of src/presentations/index.ts. verify.mjs uses that list both for `slugs.includes(reference.slug)` ('not registered') and to decide which routes to render. That is a regular expression over source text.

verify.mjs main(): `if (reference && !slugs.includes(reference.slug)) throw new CheckFailure('sample', ... not registered ...)`

criteria.rationale: I agree with Judges A and B. Three automated tests drive a browser, each by running the project's own Playwright scripts as a subprocess: tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs (runs scripts/verify.mjs), tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs (runs scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs) and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.mjs (runs `npm run verify` in a scaffolded app). A search of every *.test.* file finds no other test that uses chromium, playwright, waitForTimeout or sleep. All three files are quoted in full. None of them contains a fixed sleep. Every assertion comes after `await run(...)`, and tests/helpers.mjs `run` resolves only on the child's 'close' event. The setTimeout in `run` is a SIGKILL safety timeout that is cleared on close, not a wait. The only other setTimeout in a test (verify.test.mjs:111) is text inside an injected fault string, written into SampleScene.tsx to cause an uncaught page error. The test does not wait on it. Inside the driven script, each wait for state is a polling wait with a timeout: waitForSelector('[data-step-count]') and, after each ArrowRight, waitForFunction on data-step-index === n (verify.mjs:44-84). Judge C points to the waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) at verify.mjs:69. That call is in the verification script, not a test. It also runs only after the step index has been reached through waitForFunction and after the step index (line 59-60), title and caption (lines 61-68) have been checked. So it is not a fixed sleep used in place of waiting for a transition before asserting the step, which is the case the guidance says fails. It is a short window for catching late errors before assertClean, and nothing in the requirement depends on it. Judge C's reason therefore does not decide this criterion. In the inspect test, the `--settle` value is a minimum settle interval. Its assertions (inspect.test.mjs:92-101) check that capture waited past both the interval and the entity motion, not that a fixed delay happened.

criteria.rationale: The only acceptance exploration in the packet is round 1. It records zero product exploration steps, and says all product behavior was not exercised because the tree was unchanged. The round-0 product log it relies on is called history and is not in the packet. The seven round-0 screenshots have no capture metadata and are marked defective. The only observations of product scenarios are a few notes in the assumptions ledger: the 390x300 fit, the attribution link, the ToC aria-current state, and the present-mode toggle. Almost nothing else in the specs has a verified acceptance observation. That leaves most scenarios unobserved, including step model, entity morph and enter/exit sequencing, grouped scenes, navigation, boundary clamping, present/browse toggle, scaffold and modify flows, and verify and inspect outcomes. Only the agent-only journeys (AT-001, AT-002, AT-004) are disclosed as environmental. Skipping product behavior because the tree was unchanged is a choice, not an environment limit, so it counts against coverage.

criteria.rationale: I listed the deviations the record shows and checked each against what it surfaces. The three code-derived deviations (ENTER_DELAY shorter than the layout duration, the MIN_SCALE floor, the screenshot settle default) are ruled non-compliant in Rulings 1-3 and later recorded as fixed. The 390×300 legibility trade-off, attribution URL, ToC aria-current token, present-mode toggle visibility and Playwright pin are each recorded as questions with options and consequences. The missing implementor AXI evidence and the unverified AT-001/002/004 are also recorded. I found no observed deviation that the record leaves unsurfaced.
evidence: Rulings 1-3 identify requirement deviations and name compliant fixes.
Acceptance observation, ToC token, mode-toggle and attribution entries each give options and consequences.
Round 0/1 entries escalate the AT-001/002/004 gap.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The ledger separates what the requirements say from what the implementor chose. It states that the spec sets no MIN_SCALE value, no default settle interval and no ToC token. It identifies the implementor's tolerance and the "mostly finished" test wording as reinterpretations. It ties the attribution URL to the configured origin remote and says repository identity cannot prove owner intent. The observed 390×300 case fits and does not clip, so it is not a reproduced violation. It is described accurately as a readability trade-off, not called acceptable against a requirement. No reproduced violation is classified as acceptable.
evidence: Ruling 2 says the floor violates the SHALL-fit requirement.
The 390×300 observation says "fits its stage and does not reflow or clip" and is recorded for human review.
The attribution entry cites the origin remote as evidence.

criteria.rationale: Implementation-fixable matters (Rulings 1-3) are resolved without user decisions, with reasons given. The agent-runner gap for AT-001/002/004 is escalated and nothing is faked, which the test plan's no-mocking rule supports. The merge conflict was resolved by merging, not rebasing or force-pushing. evidence: Ruling 3 gives a compliant fix with "Pending user decision: None".

criteria.rationale: The handoff names the five open decisions by subject and points to the ledger: 390×300 legibility, attribution destination, ToC state token, mode toggle in present mode, and the Playwright pin. result.rationale: the span audit's stated contradiction was confirmed by an independent check: The timing part of the ruling holds for the newcomers wrapped in Appear. ENTER_DELAY is 0.6 + 0.05 = 0.65s. Appear applies that delay only to its own wrapper's opacity entry. Continuing entities drawn through Entity (Box) and Arrow use LAYOUT_T, 0.6s with no delay. The review guidance adds a second test, though: fail when any entity the delivered sample introduces has no entry motion at all. It says to judge every entity the sample gives a stable identity, by whatever path renders it, and to inspect each step's newly rendered entities. It also says a delayed kit path that most newcomers use does not excuse one that appears with no entry motion. E.you fails that test. The sample's own registry lists it at stage 1, next to E.prompt (entities.ts:29), so step 1 is where it is introduced. It is rendered at SampleScene.tsx:58 as a plain Box, outside any Appear. Box forwards to Entity (Box.tsx:12), and Entity sets only layout, layoutId and transition={LAYOUT_T}. It has no initial or animate opacity, so it has no entry motion. The sample does treat the other stage-1 entity as a newcomer: E.prompt is wrapped in `<Appear when={stage >= 1}>`, a condition that is always true. checks.rationale: The dissent's fact is accurate: scripts/verify.mjs calls `page.waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS)` with SETTLE_MS = 150. That fact does not settle this criterion the way the dissent claims, for two reasons. First, the criterion judges the delivered automated tests, and verify.mjs is a verification script, not a test. None of the test files contains a fixed sleep. tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs, tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.mjs make every assertion after `await run(...)`. `run` in tests/helpers.mjs resolves only on the child process's 'close' event; its setTimeout is a SIGKILL safety timer that is cleared on close. The setTimeout in verify.test.mjs is text inside an injected fault, not a wait. Second, even if the script counted, this call is not the case the guidance says fails, which is a fixed sleep for a transition before asserting the step. In renderPresentation, the step is reached through `waitForFunction` on data-step-index with a timeout. The index, title and caption are checked before the waitForTimeout runs. The sleep only leaves a short window to catch late console or page errors before `assertClean`. It does not stand in for waiting on observable state. The majority's pass reasoning stands, and the dissent does not answer it.

result.rationale: I agree with Judges A and B. Three automated tests drive a browser, each by running the project's own Playwright scripts as a subprocess: tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs (runs scripts/verify.mjs), tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs (runs scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs) and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.mjs (runs `npm run verify` in a scaffolded app). A search of every *.test.* file finds no other test that uses chromium, playwright, waitForTimeout or sleep. All three files are quoted in full. None of them contains a fixed sleep. Every assertion comes after `await run(...)`, and tests/helpers.mjs `run` resolves only on the child's 'close' event. The setTimeout in `run` is a SIGKILL safety timeout that is cleared on close, not a wait. The only other setTimeout in a test (verify.test.mjs:111) is text inside an injected fault string, written into SampleScene.tsx to cause an uncaught page error. The test does not wait on it. Inside the driven script, each wait for state is a polling wait with a timeout: waitForSelector('[data-step-count]') and, after each ArrowRight, waitForFunction on data-step-index === n (verify.mjs:44-84). Judge C points to the waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) at verify.mjs:69. That call is in the verification script, not a test. It also runs only after the step index has been reached through waitForFunction and after the step index (line 59-60), title and caption (lines 61-68) have been checked. So it is not a fixed sleep used in place of waiting for a transition before asserting the step, which is the case the guidance says fails. It is a short window for catching late errors before assertClean, and nothing in the requirement depends on it. Judge C's reason therefore does not decide this criterion. In the inspect test, the `--settle` value is a minimum settle interval. Its assertions (inspect.test.mjs:92-101) check that capture waited past both the interval and the entity motion, not that a fixed delay happened.

engineering-quality.rationale: I agree with Judges A and B. Three automated tests drive a browser, each by running the project's own Playwright scripts as a subprocess: tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs (runs scripts/verify.mjs), tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs (runs scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs) and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.mjs (runs `npm run verify` in a scaffolded app). A search of every *.test.* file finds no other test that uses chromium, playwright, waitForTimeout or sleep. All three files are quoted in full. None of them contains a fixed sleep. Every assertion comes after `await run(...)`, and tests/helpers.mjs `run` resolves only on the child's 'close' event. The setTimeout in `run` is a SIGKILL safety timeout that is cleared on close, not a wait. The only other setTimeout in a test (verify.test.mjs:111) is text inside an injected fault string, written into SampleScene.tsx to cause an uncaught page error. The test does not wait on it. Inside the driven script, each wait for state is a polling wait with a timeout: waitForSelector('[data-step-count]') and, after each ArrowRight, waitForFunction on data-step-index === n (verify.mjs:44-84). Judge C points to the waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) at verify.mjs:69. That call is in the verification script, not a test. It also runs only after the step index has been reached through waitForFunction and after the step index (line 59-60), title and caption (lines 61-68) have been checked. So it is not a fixed sleep used in place of waiting for a transition before asserting the step, which is the case the guidance says fails. It is a short window for catching late errors before assertClean, and nothing in the requirement depends on it. Judge C's reason therefore does not decide this criterion. In the inspect test, the `--settle` value is a minimum settle interval. Its assertions (inspect.test.mjs:92-101) check that capture waited past both the interval and the entity motion, not that a fixed delay happened.

audit_results.rationale: The timing part of the ruling holds for the newcomers wrapped in Appear. ENTER_DELAY is 0.6 + 0.05 = 0.65s. Appear applies that delay only to its own wrapper's opacity entry. Continuing entities drawn through Entity (Box) and Arrow use LAYOUT_T, 0.6s with no delay. The review guidance adds a second test, though: fail when any entity the delivered sample introduces has no entry motion at all. It says to judge every entity the sample gives a stable identity, by whatever path renders it, and to inspect each step's newly rendered entities. It also says a delayed kit path that most newcomers use does not excuse one that appears with no entry motion. E.you fails that test. The sample's own registry lists it at stage 1, next to E.prompt (entities.ts:29), so step 1 is where it is introduced. It is rendered at SampleScene.tsx:58 as a plain Box, outside any Appear. Box forwards to Entity (Box.tsx:12), and Entity sets only layout, layoutId and transition={LAYOUT_T}. It has no initial or animate opacity, so it has no entry motion. The sample does treat the other stage-1 entity as a newcomer: E.prompt is wrapped in `<Appear when={stage >= 1}>`, a condition that is always true. So E.you appears with no entry motion, while the entity introduced alongside it fades in. The ruling argues the first render has nothing to wait for, so E.you is never covered. But the fixture's THEN clause still requires the introduced entity to animate in, and the guidance's no-entry-motion failure does not depend on there being persisting entities. The focused test (Presentation.test.tsx:280-282) only compares the two constants and does not cover E.you. The quoted material therefore shows the requirement unmet.

audit_results.rationale: The criterion requires verification to fail when the reference sample is absent. The review guidance defines absent as not registered, or with its outline or steps content missing or out of order. The failure must be a non-zero exit at a check that reports the sample as missing or not matching the outline, and the output must name the failed phase. The quoted verifier has these checks, all labelled with the 'sample' phase. (1) After the build and before the preview starts, it fails when the reference slug is not registered in src/presentations/index.ts (verify.mjs:97-101). (2) In the and-scene package, it fails when scripts/reference-outline.json is missing (verify.mjs:28-30). (3) It fails when the rendered step count differs from the reference outline (verify.mjs:54-56). (4) It fails when any step's title or caption does not match the outline in order (verify.mjs:61-67). The top-level handler prints '[verify] FAIL (<phase>)' and sets process.exitCode = 1 (verify.mjs:123-127). This satisfies 'non-zero exit whose output names the build or sample phase'. The E2E-002 tests cover three faults: an unregistered sample, a deleted outline with the sample removed from the registry, and an out-of-order outline. Each test asserts a non-zero exit, '[verify] FAIL (sample)', and the matching message (verify.test.mjs:55-91, 128-138). The guidance does not require a dedicated test when the check is explicit, but these tests exist anyway. One edge case remains: emptying the whole OUTLINE array while keeping the sample registered. That edge case does not undercut the ruling. The quoted code gives no evidence that it would end only in an unrelated timeout: Presentation.tsx:36-45 reads step.id from steps[0], and verify.mjs:39 and 47-49 would report the uncaught page error at step 0. In any case, the guidance credits a verifier with explicit checks for a missing or mismatched sample, and those checks are quoted and tested.

first_results.rationale: Two delivered tests drive a browser: tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs and tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs. Neither drives Playwright itself. Each starts the verify or inspect script as a subprocess through run() in tests/helpers.mjs. That promise resolves only on the child's 'close' event, so every assertion runs on the finished output and report. No test sleeps for a fixed time. In helpers, setTimeout is only a 300 s SIGKILL safety timeout and is cleared on close. In verify.test.mjs, setTimeout appears only inside an injected fault string. The jsdom kit tests wait with testing-library's polling waitFor. In the browser run these tests exercise, each step is reached by waiting on state. verify.mjs waits with waitForSelector('[data-step-count]') and then waitForFunction until data-step-index equals the target step, with a timeout. Only after that does it assert the step index, title and caption. Judges A and B are borne out. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement. The page.waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) at verify.mjs:69 runs after the step index and title/caption have already been checked. It only gives late console or page errors time to arrive before assertClean(). So it is not a fixed sleep for a transition before asserting the step, which is what the guidance names. It also sits in the verify script, not in a test. That script's robustness is scored under the verification-tooling criteria, and the guidance says longer fixed settle delays earn no credit and cause no fail here.

results.rationale: I agree with Judges A and B. Three automated tests drive a browser, each by running the project's own Playwright scripts as a subprocess: tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs (runs scripts/verify.mjs), tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs (runs scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs) and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.mjs (runs `npm run verify` in a scaffolded app). A search of every *.test.* file finds no other test that uses chromium, playwright, waitForTimeout or sleep. All three files are quoted in full. None of them contains a fixed sleep. Every assertion comes after `await run(...)`, and tests/helpers.mjs `run` resolves only on the child's 'close' event. The setTimeout in `run` is a SIGKILL safety timeout that is cleared on close, not a wait. The only other setTimeout in a test (verify.test.mjs:111) is text inside an injected fault string, written into SampleScene.tsx to cause an uncaught page error. The test does not wait on it. Inside the driven script, each wait for state is a polling wait with a timeout: waitForSelector('[data-step-count]') and, after each ArrowRight, waitForFunction on data-step-index === n (verify.mjs:44-84). Judge C points to the waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) at verify.mjs:69. That call is in the verification script, not a test. It also runs only after the step index has been reached through waitForFunction and after the step index (line 59-60), title and caption (lines 61-68) have been checked. So it is not a fixed sleep used in place of waiting for a transition before asserting the step, which is the case the guidance says fails. It is a short window for catching late errors before assertClean, and nothing in the requirement depends on it. Judge C's reason therefore does not decide this criterion. In the inspect test, the `--settle` value is a minimum settle interval. Its assertions (inspect.test.mjs:92-101) check that capture waited past both the interval and the entity motion, not that a fixed delay happened.

audit_results.rationale: This pass claim says that no browser-driving test sleeps for a fixed time. Proving that needs the browser tests in full, and the quoted spans cover only parts of them. Of tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs, only lines 9-44 and 128-140 are quoted. Lines 45-127, which hold the fault definitions, are not. The claim says setTimeout appears there only inside an injected fault string, but nothing quoted shows that. Of tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs, only lines 65-101 are quoted, so the earlier helpers and any later tests are not shown. The quoted parts do look sound. tests/helpers.mjs:42-54 resolves only when the child closes, and its setTimeout is just a SIGKILL safety timer that is cleared on close. The quoted verify.mjs loop waits on state: waitForSelector and waitForFunction on data-step-index, each with a timeout. The waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) at verify.mjs:69 runs after the step index, title and caption have been checked, so it is not a fixed wait before asserting the step. But the requirement is that every browser test uses no fixed sleeps. The unquoted parts of these files could still hold a fixed sleep or an immediately-returning read used as if it waited. The material also does not show that these two files are the only browser-driving tests. These are files the judge could have cited, so this stays the judge's burden rather than missing material.

The claim says a search of every *.test.* file found no other browser test, but that search is not in the material. So it is not shown that no other browser test, or no other part of bootstrap.test.mjs, uses a fixed sleep. (2) The claim says the tests meet the 'wait for observable state' clause because of waits inside the scripts they run, citing waitForFunction in verify.mjs. The 'uncaught page error' fault test (verify.test.mjs:111) depends on that sleep to catch a setTimeout-deferred throw. The requirement says plainly 'use no fixed sleeps'. The claim counts the script's waits for the state clause but leaves out the script's sleep for the no-sleep clause, which is inconsistent. Neither script is quoted, so whether their waits are fixed sleeps or polling waits on state cannot be judged. The vitest files themselves contain no sleeps. Even so, the complete material does not decide the pass: the full set of browser tests is not established, and how the browser-driving code waits is either unquoted or includes a fixed sleep.

result.rationale: I agree with Judges A and B. Three automated tests drive a browser, each by running the project's own Playwright scripts as a subprocess: tests/e2e/verify.test.mjs (runs scripts/verify.mjs), tests/integration/inspect.test.mjs (runs scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs) and tests/integration/bootstrap.test.mjs (runs `npm run verify` in a scaffolded app). A search of every *.test.* file finds no other test that uses chromium, playwright, waitForTimeout or sleep. All three files are quoted in full. None of them contains a fixed sleep. Every assertion comes after `await run(...)`, and tests/helpers.mjs `run` resolves only on the child's 'close' event. The setTimeout in `run` is a SIGKILL safety timeout that is cleared on close, not a wait. The only other setTimeout in a test (verify.test.mjs:111) is text inside an injected fault string, written into SampleScene.tsx to cause an uncaught page error. The test does not wait on it. Inside the driven script, each wait for state is a polling wait with a timeout: waitForSelector('[data-step-count]') and, after each ArrowRight, waitForFunction on data-step-index === n (verify.mjs:44-84). Judge C points to the waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS) at verify.mjs:69. That call is in the verification script, not a test. It also runs only after the step index has been reached through waitForFunction and after the step index (line 59-60), title and caption (lines 61-68) have been checked. So it is not a fixed sleep used in place of waiting for a transition before asserting the step, which is the case the guidance says fails. It is a short window for catching late errors before assertClean, and nothing in the requirement depends on it. Judge C's reason therefore does not decide this criterion. In the inspect test, the `--settle` value is a minimum settle interval. Its assertions (inspect.test.mjs:92-101) check that capture waited past both the interval and the entity motion, not that a fixed delay happened.

engineering-quality.rationale: The criterion requires that every wait for preview readiness has a timeout. In both lib.mjs copies, startPreview's readiness wait has a 20,000 ms deadline (timeoutMs = 20000). It polls while Date.now() < deadline, then stops the preview and throws when the deadline passes. That wait has a timeout. The auditor's case needs the local preview server to accept a connection and then never respond to the fetch. The material doesn't establish that, and the guidance doesn't name it, so under the judging rules it cannot fail the criterion. If the preview process exits, the loop throws on the early exit. Refused connections are caught and retried until the deadline. The auditor concedes the build-before-preview clause is met. The printed-URL parsing clause does not apply because readiness doesn't read printed output. The stated reason does not defeat the pass.
